title: Memory: Stack & Heap
tagline: Where your variables actually live — and why confusing value with reference silently breaks code.

sections.content:
Every time you declare a variable or create an object, the runtime has to find physical space for it somewhere in RAM. That *somewhere* is not random — virtually every modern language runtime splits memory into (at least) two fundamentally different regions: the **stack** and the **heap**. Each region has its own allocation strategy, its own lifetime rules, and its own performance profile. The choice of which region holds a given value shapes nearly every aspect of how your code behaves.

Understanding the stack and heap is one of those rare topics where a single idea unlocks a dozen other things simultaneously. It explains why copying an integer is always safe while copying an object can surprise you. It explains why functions clean up after themselves automatically but forgetting to release heap memory causes memory leaks. It explains why `const` does not make an object immutable, why closures can outlive the function that created them, why recursion can crash with a stack overflow, and why garbage collectors exist at all.

This is also a perennial favourite in technical interviews — and for good reason. Engineers who understand this topic write fewer bugs, debug faster, and make better architectural decisions. The concept is simple in principle, but its implications run deep. In this chapter we will build the full picture: what each region is, how allocation and deallocation work, how JavaScript maps its types onto these regions, the mechanics of garbage collection, call-stack frames, closures and their relationship to the heap, common pitfalls, and real-world performance implications.

We will use JavaScript as our primary lens — it is the most common first language in web development — but the core ideas apply equally to Python, Java, Go, Rust, and C. Where those languages differ meaningfully, we will note why.

sections.caption: A process's memory is partitioned: the stack holds function frames (locals, return addresses) with automatic, deterministic cleanup; the heap holds objects, strings, and captured variables whose lifetime is managed by the garbage collector. Exactly which values land where is up to the engine.

sections.title: A Restaurant Kitchen and Its Walk-In Refrigerator
sections.content:
Picture a busy restaurant kitchen. Each chef (function) is assigned a numbered prep station when they start working. The station is small and neatly organised — it holds exactly what that chef needs right now: a recipe card (the return address telling the chef where to go when done), a few pre-measured bowls of ingredients (parameters and local primitives), and space for the dish taking shape. When the chef finishes, the station is wiped clean instantly and reassigned to the next cook. No one has to individually wash each bowl — the whole surface is cleared in one motion by moving a single pointer. That is the **stack**.

Now picture the walk-in refrigerator at the back of the kitchen. It is enormous. Ingredients that do not fit at any prep station — a whole leg of lamb, a 20-litre vat of stock — live here. A chef keeps a ticket slip with the fridge location of their ingredient. Multiple chefs can hold tickets pointing to the *same* item; if one chef tastes the stock and adds salt, every other chef using that same vat will find it saltier. That shared mutable access is what happens when two variables reference the same object. The kitchen manager periodically surveys the refrigerator and throws out any ingredient that no chef has a ticket for any more — that is **garbage collection**.

The key asymmetry: the prep station (stack frame) is tied to one chef's shift and vanishes when the shift ends. The walk-in fridge (heap) exists independently; items stay there until *no one* needs them.

sections.title: The Stack: Deterministic, Automatic, and Fast
sections.content:
The **call stack** is a contiguous block of memory managed with a single moving pointer called the **stack pointer**. When a function is called, the runtime **pushes** a new **stack frame** onto the stack — it moves the pointer to claim a block of memory large enough for:

- The function's **parameters** (copies of the arguments passed in — on x86-64 and ARM64 the first several arguments actually travel in registers and are only spilled to the frame when needed)
- **Local variables** declared inside the function
- The **return address** — the instruction pointer value to jump back to when the function returns
- On some architectures, the **saved frame pointer** for the calling function

When the function returns, the runtime **pops** the frame by simply moving the stack pointer back to where it was. The memory is not zeroed or individually freed; it is just abandoned in place and will be overwritten by the next push. This makes stack allocation essentially free — it is a single pointer arithmetic operation, with no searching for free space, no bookkeeping, and no per-variable cleanup.

The price of this simplicity is that the stack is **strictly LIFO**: you can only reclaim the most recently pushed frame. You cannot "free" a frame in the middle of the stack without first unwinding everything above it. This is why local variables have exactly the same lifetime as the function call that created them — no more, no less.

Each **thread** has its own stack, typically 512 KB–8 MB (8 MB for the main thread on Linux/macOS, 1 MB on Windows; V8 caps JavaScript at roughly 1 MB). The heap, by contrast, is shared by all threads of a process — which is why data races are a heap problem, and stack data is thread-private unless you leak a pointer to it. That sounds large, but each recursive call pushes a new frame. A function that calls itself a million times — or even ten thousand times on a large-frame function — will exhaust the stack and trigger a **stack overflow** error: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in JavaScript, `RecursionError` in Python (a depth counter, default limit 1000, that fires before the real stack runs out), `StackOverflowError` in Java, a segmentation fault in C.

sections.title: The Heap: Flexible, Long-Lived, and GC-Managed
sections.content:
The **heap** is a large, unstructured pool of memory — typically many hundreds of megabytes or more, limited primarily by available physical RAM and OS settings. Unlike the stack, there is no ordering constraint. You can allocate a block at any time, and it will persist until explicitly freed (in C/C++/Rust) or until the garbage collector determines it is unreachable (in Java, JavaScript, Python, Go).

Heap allocation is more expensive than stack allocation, though how much depends on the allocator:
1. **`malloc`-style allocators (C, C++, Rust)** must find a free block of the right size class (modern allocators like jemalloc/mimalloc use per-thread caches and size-class free lists), mark it used, and later accept it back via `free` — tens of nanoseconds per call, plus fragmentation.
2. **Generational GCs (V8, the JVM, .NET)** allocate new objects in the young generation by **bumping a pointer** — almost as cheap as a stack push. The real cost is paid later: every live object must be traced, copied, or compacted by the collector.

Either way, the caller gets back a **pointer** (memory address) to the new block.

In JavaScript you never call `malloc()` directly — the engine handles all of this automatically whenever you write `{}`, `[]`, or `new SomeClass()`. Allocation itself is cheap there, but every allocation brings the next garbage collection closer — which is why creating many tiny short-lived objects in a tight loop can still cost you.

Heap objects are accessed **indirectly via references**. A variable on the stack does not hold the object itself — it holds the memory address of the heap location where the object lives. Two variables can hold the same address, meaning they both point to the same chunk of heap memory. Any mutation through one pointer is immediately visible through the other, because they are both looking at the same physical bytes.

When no live variable holds a reference to a heap object — when it becomes **unreachable** — the memory it occupies is wasted until the garbage collector finds and reclaims it. The lag between an object becoming unreachable and its memory being freed is what makes heap lifetime *indefinite* rather than deterministic.

sections.title: Primitives vs. Reference Types in JavaScript
sections.content:
JavaScript divides its value types into two categories with very different memory semantics.

**Primitives** — `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `bigint` — are stored and passed **by value**. When you assign a primitive to a new variable, the new variable behaves as an independent copy: nothing you do through one variable can affect the other. (Primitives are immutable, so there is no way to "modify" a primitive in place — you can only rebind a variable to a different value.)

**Value semantics is not the same as "lives on the stack".** Where the bits physically sit is an engine detail. In V8, small integers (**Smis**) are stored directly inside the tagged value, but strings, BigInts, and non-small numbers (**HeapNumbers** such as `1.5`) are heap objects — assigning a string copies a pointer to the same immutable string, which is safe precisely because it can never change. The same split exists elsewhere: Java's `Integer` and C#'s boxed values live on the heap, while a C# `struct` or Swift `struct` that is a field of a class lives inside that heap object. Think of stack vs. heap as *lifetime and allocation strategy*, and value vs. reference as *copy semantics*.

**Objects, arrays, and functions** — everything that is not a primitive — are **reference types**. The value that sits in a variable is not the object itself but a **reference**: a numeric memory address pointing to the object on the heap. When you assign a reference-type variable to another variable, only the reference (the address) is copied, not the heap data it points to. Both variables end up referencing the same object.

This distinction has huge practical consequences:
- Passing a primitive to a function is always safe from the caller's perspective — the function gets its own copy.
- Passing an object to a function gives the function access to the same heap data. A function that mutates `obj.count` modifies the original object seen by the caller.
- Comparison with `===` for objects tests reference equality ("are these the same object in memory?"), not structural equality ("do these objects have the same contents?"). Two objects with identical properties return `false` from `===` if they occupy different heap addresses.

sections.explanation: The first block shows that primitives copy their value. The second shows that objects share a reference — user2 is an alias for user1, not a copy. Reference equality (===) tests the address, not content. The function example shows the real-world danger: addBonus() modifies the caller's data because it received a reference, not a copy. Strings are heap-allocated in V8 yet behave like values because they are immutable — methods always return new strings, never mutate in place.

sections.title: Shallow vs. Deep Cloning: Why Spread Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Because assignment copies references, developers often want to **clone** an object to get an independent copy. There are three levels of copying to understand:

**1. Reference copy (alias):** `const b = a;` — single heap object, two references. Any mutation through either is shared.

**2. Shallow clone:** `const b = { ...a };` or `Object.assign({}, a)` — creates a new top-level heap object and copies each of `a`'s own enumerable property *values* into it. If those values are primitives, they are truly copied. If they are themselves references (nested objects or arrays), only the references are copied — `a` and `b` now share the same nested heap objects. Mutating a nested object through `b` still affects `a`.

**3. Deep clone:** `const b = structuredClone(a);` — recursively creates new heap objects for every level of nesting. After a deep clone, `a` and `b` are completely independent trees. `structuredClone()` (available in all modern browsers and Node 17+) handles arrays, Maps, Sets, Dates, RegExps, typed arrays, and circular references. It **throws** a `DataCloneError` on functions and DOM nodes, and it copies class instances as **plain objects** — the prototype (and therefore its methods) is lost.

For JSON-safe data, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(a))` is the classic deep-clone hack — cheap to remember but has pitfalls: it drops `undefined` values and functions, converts `Date` objects to strings, turns `NaN`/`Infinity` into `null` and `Map`/`Set` into `{}`, and throws on `BigInt` values and circular references.

Knowing which level of copying you need is a key skill. Most bugs come from accidentally sharing a reference when you intended independence.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The first block demonstrates the shallow-clone trap: the top-level `id` (a primitive) is truly copied, but `address` (a reference) is shared, so renaming the city through `shallow` changes `original` too. `structuredClone()` then produces a fully independent tree. The last two blocks show the JSON trick and its two most common failure modes: `undefined` values are silently dropped and `Date` objects become ISO strings.

sections.title: const, Immutability, and Object.freeze()
sections.content:
`const` is perhaps the most widely misunderstood keyword in JavaScript, and the misunderstanding maps directly to stack-vs-heap confusion.

`const` creates a **binding** — an association between a name and a value — that cannot be **reassigned**. For primitives, that means the value itself cannot change: `const n = 5; n = 6;` throws a `TypeError`. For objects, the *reference* (heap address) stored in the binding is what cannot change. The heap object it points to is entirely mutable: `const arr = [1,2,3]; arr.push(4);` works perfectly because `arr` (the reference) still points to the same heap array — you are mutating the array's *contents*, not reassigning the variable.

To actually lock heap data, you need explicit immutability tools:

- **`Object.freeze(obj)`**: makes all of `obj`'s own properties (enumerable or not) non-writable and non-configurable, and prevents new properties from being added. In strict mode, attempting to write throws a `TypeError`; in sloppy mode, the write is silently ignored. Freeze is **shallow** — nested objects are not frozen and can still be mutated.

- **Deep freeze**: requires a recursive function that calls `Object.freeze()` on every nested object. There is no built-in deep freeze.

- **Immutable data libraries**: libraries like Immer (used by Redux Toolkit) let you write code that *looks* like mutation but produces new immutable objects behind the scenes, using structural sharing to avoid copying unchanged branches.

The practical rule: use `const` for everything by default (it prevents accidental reassignment). When you need true immutability, use `Object.freeze()` for simple cases or Immer for complex state trees.

sections.title: Garbage Collection: How the Heap Cleans Itself
sections.content:
In languages like C and C++, the programmer allocates heap memory with `malloc()` and must free it with `free()`. Forgetting to free causes a **memory leak** — heap memory accumulates as the program runs until the OS eventually kills the process. Freeing memory too early causes **use-after-free** bugs — reading or writing deallocated memory, leading to crashes or security vulnerabilities. Manual memory management is powerful but notoriously error-prone.

JavaScript (and Python, Java, Go, C#) solve this with **automatic garbage collection (GC)**. The programmer never calls `free()`; the runtime tracks which heap objects are reachable and periodically reclaims those that are not.

**Mark-and-sweep** is the foundational GC algorithm used (in various refined forms) by V8, SpiderMonkey, and most managed-language runtimes:

1. **Mark phase**: Starting from a set of **GC roots** — global variables, stack variables in active frames, and CPU registers — the collector traverses every reference chain. Every object reachable by following references from roots is marked as live.

2. **Sweep phase**: The collector scans the entire heap. Any object not marked as live is considered garbage and its memory is returned to the free pool.

Modern GCs are far more sophisticated than a naive mark-and-sweep:
- **Generational GC**: most objects die young — they are allocated, used briefly, and quickly become unreachable. V8 splits the heap into a **young generation** ("nursery") and an **old generation**. Minor GC runs frequently on the small nursery; major GC ("full" or "old-gen") runs less often. This dramatically reduces pauses.
- **Incremental and concurrent GC**: instead of stopping the world for a full mark-and-sweep, modern GCs do most marking and sweeping on background threads while the program runs, so main-thread pauses are typically a few milliseconds or less.
- **Compaction**: after collecting garbage, the GC can move live objects together (compaction), reducing heap fragmentation and improving cache locality.

**What this means for your code**: you can accidentally create **memory leaks in JavaScript** by holding references longer than needed — especially through global variables, event listeners that are never removed, closures that capture more than intended, or long-lived data structures that accumulate entries never removed.

flowchart TD
  R["GC Roots\n(globals · stack frames · registers)"] --> O1["Object A\n(reachable — LIVE)"]
  O1 --> O2["Object B\n(reachable — LIVE)"]
  O1 --> O3["Object C\n(reachable — LIVE)"]
  O4["Object D\n(unreachable — GARBAGE)"]

sections.title: Value vs. Reference in Function Arguments: Pass by Value of the Reference

sections.content: **Historical and cross-language context:** The stack-and-heap separation is not specific to JavaScript. In **C/C++**, every local variable goes on the stack by default; you use `malloc()`/`new` explicitly for heap allocation and `free()`/`delete` to reclaim it. In **Rust**, ownership and the borrow checker guarantee at compile time that heap data is freed exactly once and never used after freeing — eliminating use-after-free and double-free bugs without a GC, at the cost of a steeper learning curve. (Leaks are still possible and considered memory-safe: `Rc` reference cycles or `std::mem::forget`.) In **Python**, all objects — even small integers and strings — are heap-allocated reference-counted objects (CPython uses reference counting plus a cycle collector). In **Go**, the compiler performs **escape analysis**: if a local variable's address escapes the function (e.g., is returned or stored in a global), the compiler automatically allocates it on the heap; otherwise it stays on the stack. Java's JIT does something similar at runtime (escape analysis with scalar replacement), and C#/Swift `struct`s are value types that live inline wherever they are stored — on the stack as locals, inside the heap object when they are a field of a class. The trade-offs between GC, reference counting, and manual management are a major dimension along which languages differ.

**Interview insight — what interviewers actually want to hear:**

When asked 'what is the difference between the stack and the heap?', lead with **lifetime and management**, not just speed:

- Stack: automatic, deterministic lifetime tied to function-call scope; freed on return; LIFO; fast; fixed size; **one per thread**.
- Heap: indefinite lifetime; freed explicitly or when GC detects no live references; arbitrary allocation order; slower to allocate and reclaim; much larger; **shared by all threads** (hence locks and data races).

Then connect to JavaScript specifics: primitives are value types (copied on assignment), objects are reference types (reference is copied, heap data is shared). Mention that `const` prevents reference reassignment but does not freeze heap data.

Bonus points: mention closures as the mechanism that moves stack variables to the heap when they need to outlive their frame. Mention generational GC as why creating many short-lived objects can still be relatively efficient in V8.

Common wrong answer to avoid: 'the stack is fast and the heap is slow, therefore use the stack' — in JavaScript you do not choose where values go; the engine decides (based on type, closure capture, and escape analysis). The insight is understanding the *consequences* of that choice.

items: The **stack** is a small, fast, LIFO region — one per thread. Each call pushes a frame (parameters, locals, return address) that is reclaimed instantly on return; allocation is a single pointer move.

The **heap** is a large, flexible region for data that must outlive a single function call. Objects are allocated here and persist until the garbage collector determines no live reference reaches them.

JavaScript **primitives** (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) have **value semantics** — assignment behaves like a copy because primitives are immutable. That is about copy semantics, not location: V8 keeps strings, BigInts, and non-small numbers on the heap.

JavaScript **objects, arrays, and functions** are heap-allocated reference types — variables hold memory addresses. Assigning or passing an object copies the address, creating an alias; mutations through any alias affect the shared heap object.

`const` prevents **reference reassignment** only. The heap object a `const` variable points to is freely mutable. Use `Object.freeze()` for shallow immutability or `structuredClone()` for a fully independent deep copy.

**Closures** capture variables onto the heap so they outlive the function frame that created them. This enables private state and functional patterns but can cause memory leaks if closures unintentionally keep large objects reachable.

The **garbage collector** reclaims heap memory by reachability: starting from GC roots (globals, stack frames, registers), it marks reachable objects and reclaims the rest. V8's generational GC allocates by bumping a pointer and does most marking/sweeping concurrently, keeping main-thread pauses to a few milliseconds or less.
Closures in V8 keep captured variables in a heap **Context** shared by all closures from that scope — one long-lived closure can keep a large captured object alive even if it never uses it.

quiz.question: Where are a function's local primitive variables stored during execution?
options: In the stack frame for that function call
On the heap, managed by the garbage collector
In a global memory region shared by all functions
In CPU registers only, never in RAM
quiz.explanation: Conceptually, each function call pushes a stack frame that holds its locals and parameters (engines may keep them in registers, and a local captured by a closure moves to the heap). The frame is popped and freed the instant the function returns — no GC involvement needed.

quiz.question: After `const user1 = { score: 10 }; const user2 = user1; user2.score = 99;`, what is `user1.score`?
options: 10 — user1 is protected by const
99 — user1 and user2 reference the same heap object
undefined — user1 was reassigned
A TypeError is thrown because user2 is const
quiz.explanation: user1 and user2 both hold the same heap address. Mutating through user2 changes the shared heap object. const only prevents reassigning the reference — it does not freeze the heap data.

quiz.question: What does `structuredClone(obj)` do that `{ ...obj }` does not?
options: It freezes the resulting object so it cannot be mutated
It converts the object to JSON and back
It copies the prototype chain and class methods
It recursively deep-copies all nested objects, producing a fully independent tree
quiz.explanation: Spread ({ ...obj }) is a shallow clone — nested objects are still shared references. structuredClone() recursively copies all levels, so the clone and the original are completely independent. It also handles circular references, Maps, Sets, and Dates correctly.

quiz.question: What does the garbage collector use to decide whether a heap object can be reclaimed?
options: How long the object has been alive in milliseconds
The size of the object in bytes
Whether any live reference chain from a GC root reaches the object
Whether the variable was declared with let or const
quiz.explanation: JavaScript's GC uses reachability (mark-and-sweep). An object is collected only when no live path from a root — global, stack variable, or active closure — leads to it. Age and size do not determine collectability.

quiz.question: Why does `const arr = [1, 2, 3]; arr.push(4);` not throw a TypeError?
options: Arrays are special — const does not apply to them
push() creates a new array, so arr is not modified
const only prevents reassigning the reference; mutating the heap array through push() is allowed
const is only enforced in strict mode
quiz.explanation: const prevents arr = somethingElse (reassigning the binding). It does not prevent modifying the heap array that arr points to. push() mutates the existing array in place, which is perfectly legal.

quiz.question: What is the most likely cause of a 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' (RangeError) in JavaScript?
options: Allocating a very large array on the heap
Infinite or very deep recursion exhausting the call stack
Mutating a const variable
Calling JSON.parse on an invalid string
quiz.explanation: Each function call pushes a stack frame. Unbounded recursion keeps pushing frames until the thread's stack size limit (typically 1-8 MB) is exceeded — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: A closure captures a large array in an event listener that is never removed. What memory problem can this cause?
options: Stack overflow, because the array uses too much stack space
No problem — the GC detects this pattern and collects the array anyway
A TypeError, because event listeners cannot capture variables
A memory leak, because the closure keeps the array reachable and the GC cannot collect it
quiz.explanation: As long as the event listener is registered, the closure holds a reference to the array, making it reachable from a GC root (the event target). The GC will never collect it, causing heap memory to grow indefinitely — a classic JavaScript memory leak.

quiz.question: You call `function tryReplace(obj) { obj = { x: 99 }; }` with an object argument. After the call, what happens to the caller's variable?
options: The caller's variable now points to the new object { x: 99 }
The caller's variable is unchanged — only the local copy of the reference was reassigned
The original object is mutated to have x: 99
A TypeError is thrown because obj is const inside the function
quiz.explanation: JavaScript passes a copy of the reference. Reassigning obj inside the function only changes the local copy; the caller's variable still holds the original heap address. To affect the caller, you must mutate the object's properties, not reassign obj.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript primitive is stored by value when assigned to a new variable?
options: An array []
A plain object {}
A boolean true/false
A function () => {}
quiz.explanation: Booleans are primitives — they are copied by value. Arrays, plain objects, and functions are all heap-allocated reference types; assignment copies the reference, not the data.

quiz.question: After `const cfg = Object.freeze({ host: 'localhost', port: 3000 }); cfg.port = 9999;`, what is the outcome?
options: 3000 — the write is silently ignored (sloppy mode) or throws TypeError (strict mode)
9999 — Object.freeze only affects future Object.freeze calls
undefined — freeze removes all property values
A ReferenceError is thrown because cfg is const
quiz.explanation: Object.freeze() makes the object's own properties non-writable. In sloppy mode the write is silently ignored and cfg.port remains 3000. In strict mode a TypeError is thrown. Either way, cfg.port is 3000 if the code continues — not 9999.
